A slow morning in Luxembourg Gardens before spending six hours getting lost in the Louvre. Fueled, as all good days in Paris should be, by pastries and sandwiches. Also including an unreasonable amount of walking.
Naming: `Place/{Name}`, e.g. `Place/Palace of Fine Arts`, `Place/Lake Louise`, `Place/Colonia del Sacramento`.
Anchor: a place personally encountered in travel that is worth preserving visually and descriptively.

Boundary: if the primary point is the historical event associated with the place → Annals and Histories. If the primary point is a person connected to the place → Plutarch. If the entry is really about the trip or route as a whole rather than one place → the Travel Sketchbook structure page should hold that itinerary context. A `Place/` tag may appear in multiple patterns. Tacitus and Chreia reference places where events occurred; Gerald creates canonical Place/ pages for personally visited sites. Use the finest-grained Place that merits its own page. A city-level Place (e.g. `Place/Rome`) may be referenced by Tacitus and also have child Place pages created by Gerald (e.g. `Place/Colosseum`). No conflict.
Tags: `Place/`, `Concept/`, and `Theme/` required; `Time/{year}`; `Country/`, `Region/`, or `City/` as useful; `Person/`, `Event/`, `Source/` when relevant. Also tag `Kind/` (see options below):
Garden: link from the Travel Sketchbook structure under the relevant journey, region, or geographic section.
Add to the Lab index page.
Cross-domain use: link to historical events, persons, concepts, sources, or other structures when the place supports later synthesis.
Privacy: prefer places, landscapes, buildings, streets, objects, and environmental details over identifiable family photographs for the public site. People may remain incidental where appropriate.
Posture: this is a topographical plate, not a travel essay. Preserve what made the place visually, historically, atmospherically, or personally distinctive.
Whimsy: unusual details, legends, rumors, mistaken impressions, overheard remarks, or family sayings are welcome when they help preserve the character of the place.
View = the original photograph or selected image of the place.
Plate = sketch or illustrated rendering derived from the View; It should simplify or interpret the view without inventing major features that were not present.
Place = name, location, and identifying context.
Date = when the place was visited.
Features = short list of the visual or physical elements that define the scene.

Observation = what was actually noticed there: atmosphere, scale, texture, light, architecture, landscape, sound, weather, or other concrete impressions; write from actual encounter first. Historical context, local stories, hearsay, oddities, and remembered remarks may be included, but distinguish clearly between what was personally observed, what was learned later, and what belongs to local lore.
Context = historical, cultural, geographical, architectural, or natural background that makes the place more intelligible.
Memory = the personal circumstance of encountering the place: what was happening, what stood out, what the family noticed, or why the place remained memorable.
Lore = optional legends, hearsay, local stories, oddities, rumors, or notable anecdotes connected to the place.
Significance = why this place deserves to remain in the collection rather than as an ordinary travel photograph.

Marie de' Medici had the Luxembourg grotto built around 1630, modeled after the nymphaea and fountains that decorated Italian gardens. Since then it has been known as the "Medici Fountain." Thomas Francini, Intendant General of Waters and Fountains of the King, is said to have drawn up the plans.

Built against the structures that it concealed, the fountain formed, to the east, the end of the long vista running alongside the palace. Its facade consisted of three niches separated by columns adorned with bosses and shell decorations, and was crowned by a pediment bearing the arms of France and the Medici. It was decorated with river figures commissioned from the sculptor Pierre Biard. On either side it continued into a wall decorated with arcades.
Chalgrin, architect of the Luxembourg Palace, restored it after the Revolution with the sculptors Ramey, Duret, and Talamona, and decorated the central niche with a small Venus.

In 1862, Haussmann's construction of the Rue de Médicis caused the fountain to be moved about thirty meters closer to the palace. The architect Alphonse de Gisors then had the long basin, about fifty meters in length, constructed in front of it and commissioned new sculptures from Ottin.

The central niche is occupied by the group representing "Polyphemus Surprising Acis and Galatea," while the two side niches contain a faun and a huntress. The rear facade consists of a bas-relief, created in 1807 by Valois for the former fountain on the Rue du Regard, topped by two graceful naiads by the sculptor Klagmann.

The central sculpture comes from Book XIII of [[Ovid]]'s [[Metamorphoses]]. Galatea is a Nereid, a sea nymph and daughter of Nereus. Galatea is in love with [[Acis]], a handsome young Sicilian shepherd. But [[Polyphemus]], the enormous one-eyed Cyclops (from the [[Odyssey]]), has fallen desperately in love with her.

Ovid makes Polyphemus surprisingly comic at first. Love has turned this terrifying monster into an awkward suitor. He starts worrying about his appearance. He combs his coarse hair, trims his beard, looks at himself in the water, and composes a long love song for Galatea. He boasts about his livestock, his cave, his fruit trees, his milk and cheese, and even two bear cubs he has saved as a present for her.

But the comedy gradually becomes threatening. Polyphemus knows Galatea prefers Acis, and his love is intensely possessive. In the same song in which he declares his love for her, he fantasizes about tearing Acis apart.

This brings us to the precise moment depicted by the Medici Fountain. The lovers lie beneath the rock while the enormous Polyphemus stands above them, preparing to throw the stone that will kill Acis.
Polyphemus discovers Acis and Galatea together. Galatea escapes into the sea. Acis runs, but Polyphemus tears a massive piece of rock from the mountain and hurls it at him. The rock crushes Acis.

Galatea cannot restore him to human life. Instead, she uses her divine power so that his blood becomes water. In Ovid's telling, the blood beneath the rock gradually changes into a stream; reeds emerge, water gushes through a crack in the rock, and Acis reappears as a river god. From then on, he continues to exist as the Sicilian river bearing his name.

The peacefulness of the fountain catches you off guard after walking through the surrounding streets of Paris. Then, you read the description on the sign and learn that the tranquil garden fountain ends in a rather violent mythological scene of the jealous Cyclops Polyphemus discovering Galatea with Acis. Leave it to the French to make a murder scene picturesque and peaceful.

The Gardens of Versailles were transformed for Louis XIV beginning in 1661, principally by landscape architect André Le Nôtre. Covering roughly 2,000 acres, they were conceived as an extension of the palace itself, with immense sightlines, geometric parterres, carefully shaped trees, sculptures, canals, and hundreds of fountains imposing order on the landscape.

Much of the garden's character comes from its bosquets, enclosed outdoor "rooms" hidden behind hedges. Visitors moving through them would suddenly encounter fountains, sculptures, theaters, and other surprises. The scale created unusual engineering challenges too, especially supplying enough water for the fountains, leading to ambitious reservoirs, aqueducts, pumping systems, and the enormous Machine de Marly on the Seine. Louis XIV was so particular about how the gardens should be experienced that he personally wrote instructions prescribing the route visitors should take through them.
One of the most interesting things about the Gardens of Versailles is that they were essentially a massive engineering project disguised as a garden.

Louis XIV wanted an astonishing number of fountains, but Versailles sits on relatively flat ground and had no adequate natural water supply. Engineers eventually built the enormous Machine de Marly, a system of waterwheels and pumps on the Seine, to help supply Versailles.

Even then, there often wasn't enough water to run all the fountains simultaneously. During Louis XIV's walks, fountain keepers reportedly coordinated with one another so that the fountains near the king were turned on as he approached and shut off after he passed. Even nature itself was made to appear ordered around the king.

I remember sitting in the gardens at Versailles watching the fountains move in time with the music. Each display was relatively short, almost like a little performance scattered throughout the gardens. We'd stop, watch the water rise and fall with the music, and then wander on to find the next one.
